Dental procedure discomfort

A small crossover study reported lower pain and tiredness after PBM during a simulated mouth-open procedure. Clinical relevance to actual dental care is uncertain.

PBM Database summary

What the records report

A small crossover study reported lower pain and tiredness after PBM during a simulated mouth-open procedure. Clinical relevance to actual dental care is uncertain.

Summary of the Evidence

One 16-participant randomized placebo-controlled crossover study is indexed under the related category “Dental treatment comfort”; it simulated a prolonged procedure by keeping the mouth open for 50 minutes rather than testing PBM during actual dental care. No animal or in-vitro/ex-vivo study is listed.

Human and clinical evidence

Participants reported lower pain and tiredness after PBM than placebo. Because the model was simulated, outcomes were subjective, and the database flags uncertainty in the crossover description, this is preliminary evidence only (Bitencourt et al. 2021). Because this is a simulated setting, the study does not directly test discomfort during drilling, injections, surgery, or a complete dental appointment. The crossover design lets each participant receive active and placebo sessions, but the sample of 16 and subjective outcomes leave estimates imprecise; a temperature difference is a physiological measure, not proof of pain relief by itself. Replication during real clinical procedures is needed before applying the result to routine care.

Primary original study: Bitencourt et al. 2021

Animal evidence

none identified.

In-vitro and ex-vivo evidence

none identified.

Treatment Parameters and Generalizability

The study used 786 nm near-infrared light at 9 J per point and 100 mW. Discomfort was induced by keeping the mouth open during a simulated 50-minute procedure. This wavelength is outside the visible band. These settings and subjective outcomes describe the experimental model, not a validated regimen for actual dental procedures.

Interpretation

The crossover design allows within-participant comparison, but the study included only 32 volunteers and did not test care delivery in a dental clinic. Thermographic temperature is a physiological measure and does not by itself establish patient benefit. Larger studies during real procedures are needed before generalizing the finding.

Evidence strength in source summaryVery low. One small crossover study used a simulated procedure rather than dental treatment.

Evidence strength rationale and next steps

A single randomized crossover study used a simulated 50-minute dental procedure and measured self-reported pain and tiredness. Participants reported lower discomfort after PBM, but the setting was not a real dental procedure and the sample was small. Clinical effects during drilling, injections, or surgery remain untested by this report.
